abstract: | 
 The Chilean social unrest of October 2019 poses a paradox for political theory: Why did highly educated sectors—typically associated with democratic moderation—legitimize forms of disruptive violence? Using longitudinal data from ELSOC (2016–2023; 20,007 observations, 3,666 individuals), this article examines the relationship between educational attainment, participation in protests, and the justification of violence through multilevel models. The results challenge the "civilizing effect" of education: among non-participants, higher education reduces the justification of violence; among protesters, it significantly increases it. Mobilized university students exhibit the highest levels, reversing the expected effect. This pattern reflects a moral duality: educated participants reject state violence while legitimizing protest violence, thereby developing differentiated normative frameworks. These findings explain how the cross-sectional nature of the Chilean movement emerged from the rearticulation of moral frameworks across professional sectors, with implications for the study of nonviolent radicalization, political socialization, and the legitimacy of transgression in democracies with structural inequality. 

 **Keywords**: Protests · Violence · Stratification · Attitudes · Chile
